notes.meaning: Jonathan was not with his father when Saul made the soldiers swear to fast. Because he was exhausted from fighting, Jonathan dipped his staff into wild honey and ate it. The sugar instantly restored his energy and cleared the dimness from his eyes caused by extreme hunger.
A soldier saw Jonathan eat and warned him about the king's strict command. Saul had placed a curse on anyone who ate before evening, leaving the entire army starving and weak in the middle of battle.

Jonathan pointed out that his father's command had brought trouble rather than help to Israel. His own refreshed sight was clear proof that a little nourishment gave much-needed strength for the fight.

Jonathan explained that the army could have won a far greater victory if they had been allowed to eat captured food. Denying food to tired soldiers only slowed the pursuit and allowed more enemies to escape. Foolish human rules often ruin the very success a leader hopes to achieve.
The Israelites chased the Philistines about twenty miles, all the way from Michmash down to Aijalon. By the end of this long chase over rough hills, the soldiers were completely drained of strength.

As soon as evening arrived and the vow ended, the starving soldiers threw themselves wildly upon the captured livestock. Because they were famished, they slaughtered the animals directly on the ground and ate the meat without draining the blood, directly violating God's law.

When Saul was told that the troops were sinning against the Lord by eating meat with blood in it, he accused them of breaking faith. He ordered a massive stone rolled over to serve as an elevated butchering block so the blood could properly drain into the earth. Saul quickly blamed the people for their sin while ignoring that his own rash fast had driven them to it.

Saul sent officers through the camp telling every soldier to bring his animal to the large stone to be killed properly under supervision. The troops obeyed and brought their cattle through the night, ending the sinful practice. This showed that Saul cared about keeping religious rules, even though his earlier bad decision had created the crisis.

Saul then built an altar to the Lord, which the text notes was the very first altar he had ever built. He may have set it up to thank God for the day's victory, or to seek forgiveness for the army's sin. It highlights that Saul had ruled for some time before ever taking the initiative to honor God with an altar.

Once the men were fed, Saul proposed marching throughout the night to wipe out the Philistines completely. The weary soldiers agreed to whatever the king wanted, but the priest urged everyone to ask God for direction first before rushing into danger.

Saul asked God whether Israel should attack the Philistines and if He would hand them over, but God gave no answer at all. When the sacred stones used by the priest gave no response, it meant God was withholding His favor. Saul assumed this silence was caused by someone hiding a sin.

Saul called all the military leaders together to find out what sin had caused God to remain silent. Instead of questioning his own actions, the king assumed that a soldier's hidden disobedience had brought God's displeasure on the camp.

Saul rashly swore by the living Lord that the guilty person would be put to death, even if it turned out to be his own son Jonathan. The soldiers who knew Jonathan had eaten honey stayed completely silent because they loved Jonathan and wanted to protect him.
Saul set up a formal test to find the offender, placing all the troops on one side and standing with Jonathan on the other. The people passively agreed to let him do whatever seemed best to him.
Saul prayed for God to reveal who was guilty by guiding the sacred lots. The lot cleared the army of any guilt and pointed straight at Saul and Jonathan.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern translations follow ancient Greek manuscripts that preserve a longer prayer where Saul asks God to reveal the culprit through the Urim and Thummim, rather than the shorter traditional Hebrew reading.

notes.meaning: The lots were cast again, this time between the king and his son, and the lot singled out Jonathan. God allowed the lot to identify Jonathan not because eating honey was a sin in God's eyes, but to expose the danger and folly of Saul's reckless oath.

Saul commanded Jonathan to confess what he had done, and Jonathan plainly told the truth. He explained that he had only tasted a little honey from the tip of his staff, amazed that he was expected to die for such a harmless act done in ignorance.

Saul pronounced an unconditional death sentence upon his son, calling down a curse on himself if he failed to execute Jonathan. He put the pride of keeping his foolish words above the life of his faithful son.

differ.view: Saul was acting out of a genuine, though mistaken, fear of God by valuing his solemn oath more than his natural family affection.

notes.meaning: The army firmly stood up to the king and refused to let Jonathan be harmed. They swore by the Lord that not a single hair of his head would fall, because God had clearly worked through Jonathan to bring Israel a great victory that day. The people successfully rescued Jonathan from his father's sentence.

After Jonathan was spared, Saul called off the nighttime chase against the Philistines, allowing the remaining enemy troops to escape back to their own land. Saul's foolish oath and family turmoil cost Israel the chance to completely break the Philistine threat.

Once Saul firmly secured his royal authority over the nation, he fought off hostile neighbors on every border. He pushed back Moab, Ammon, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines, giving Israel relief from constant attacks.

Saul fought bravely and defeated the Amalekites, a wandering desert people who had raided Israelite towns for generations. This campaign helped rescue God's people from bands of robbers who constantly looted their land.
The text lists Saul's three sons who fought beside him: Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. It also names his two daughters, Merab, the older, and Michal, the younger.

Saul's wife was Ahinoam, and the commander of his army was his cousin Abner. Abner's father Ner and Saul's father Kish were both sons of a man named Abiel. Keeping high military posts in the hands of trusted family members was a common way kings secured their rule.

Israel faced continuous, brutal warfare against the Philistines throughout Saul's entire life. Whenever the king spotted an exceptionally strong or courageous warrior, he drafted him into his royal army to keep his fighting force ready.
